summaryEn: At Haeinsa Temple, Hoya discovers the Tripitaka Koreana: more than 80,000 woodblocks of Buddhist scriptures carved between 1237 and 1248, still kept safe today.
learningGoalsEn: Know that the Tripitaka Koreana (Palmandaejanggyeong) is a set of more than 80,000 woodblocks of Buddhist scriptures carved in Goryeo between 1237 and 1248.
Understand why the blocks were carved: a wish for the Buddha's protection during the Mongol invasions.
Know that the woodblocks are kept at Haeinsa Temple and were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.
Read and recognize 해인사 (Haeinsa), 대장경 (Daejanggyeong), 팔만 (palman), 나무 (namu), 경판 (gyeongpan) and 글자 (geulja).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

review.advisoryNoteEn: Mentions that Mongol armies invaded Korea long ago. No fighting is shown.

keywords.en: Goryeo, the Korean kingdom of that time

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya climbs Gayasan Mountain to Haeinsa Temple in Hapcheon. Peeking through the slats of a long wooden hall, he gasps. Shelves of carved wooden blocks stretch on, row after row!
scenes.artBrief: Hoya on a forest path up a green mountain toward a temple with tiled roofs; inset: a long dim hall with tall wooden shelves packed with dark wooden blocks seen through vertical window slats.

art.altEn: Hoya climbs to Haeinsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain and peeks at a long wooden hall full of carved woodblocks.

scenes.narrationEn: These are the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks. In Korean they are called Daejanggyeong, which means a complete collection of Buddhist scriptures.

keyword.en: the complete collection of Buddhist scriptures (Tripitaka)

scenes.artBrief: Rows of wooden printing blocks on shelves, each with small end pieces; warm light falls across them; Hoya stands small and amazed in the aisle. Block faces shown as texture, no readable characters.

art.altEn: Hoya stands amazed between shelves packed with the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, a complete collection of Buddhist scriptures.

scenes.narrationEn: They were carved in the Goryeo kingdom, from 1237 to 1248. Mongol armies had invaded the land, and people carved the scriptures hoping the Buddha's power would protect their country.

keyword.en: Goryeo, the Korean kingdom of that time

scenes.artBrief: Calm workshop scene: carvers in Goryeo clothing bent over wooden boards with small knives, focused and peaceful; distant mountains outside. No fighting, no soldiers.

art.altEn: In Goryeo, from 1237 to 1248, carvers kneel calmly over wooden boards, cutting the scriptures with small knives.

scenes.captionEn: Carved in Goryeo, hoping for protection

scenes.narrationEn: There are more than 80,000 blocks, which is one reason people call them Palman Daejanggyeong. Palman means eighty thousand! Hoya starts counting, then laughs. "That would take me all year!"
scenes.artBrief: Hoya sitting on the floor counting on his paws, dizzy little stars circling his head, with endless shelves of blocks behind him.

art.altEn: Hoya tries to count the more than 80,000 woodblocks on the shelves behind him, then laughs.

scenes.narrationEn: Each block, a {kw:gyeongpan}, is carved on both sides. Most are made of wild cherry wood, coated with lacquer to protect them, and fitted with metal plates at the corners.
scenes.artBrief: A single woodblock shown large, tilted to reveal both carved faces as abstract texture, dark lacquer sheen, and small metal plates at the four corners; a cherry tree in blossom behind it.

art.altEn: One woodblock, carved on both sides, lacquered and fitted with metal corner plates, with a wild cherry tree in blossom behind it.

scenes.captionEn: Each block is carved on both sides

scenes.narrationEn: Carvers cut tens of millions of characters into the wood, all neat and even, as if one hand had carved them all. Scholars around the world praise how accurate they are.
scenes.artBrief: Close-up of a carver's steady hands and a small knife over a board covered in tiny, even raised marks (abstract pattern, not real characters); Hoya watches, holding his breath.

art.altEn: A carver cuts tiny, even characters into a board with a small knife, and Hoya watches, holding his breath.

scenes.captionEn: Tens of millions of neat characters

scenes.narrationEn: Today the woodblocks are a National Treasure of Korea. In 2007, UNESCO added them to the Memory of the World Register.
scenes.artBrief: Hoya proudly standing beside a single woodblock displayed on a cushion, with a soft starburst behind it suggesting world recognition. No logos or text.

art.altEn: Hoya stands proudly beside a glowing woodblock: the blocks are a National Treasure and on the Memory of the World Register.

scenes.captionEn: A National Treasure, honored by UNESCO

scenes.narrationEn: Almost 800 years later, the blocks are still kept safe at Haeinsa. Hoya whispers, "Sojunghaeyo, they're precious."

approximations.rationaleEn: The blocks were finished in 1248; 1248 to 2026 is 778 years, so narration rounds it to almost 800.

scenes.artBrief: Evening at Haeinsa: the long storage halls glowing softly at the top of the temple grounds under a starry sky; Hoya sits quietly on the steps.

art.altEn: In the evening the long storage halls of Haeinsa rest under the stars, and Hoya waits quietly in front of them.

To sell them at the market

To ask the Buddha to protect the land

facts.claimEn: There are more than 80,000 blocks. UNESCO's Memory of the World record gives 81,258; the Korea Heritage Service notes that this figure comes from a survey made under Japanese rule and includes some blocks re-carved in Joseon. This is one reason the set is called Palman ('eighty thousand') Daejanggyeong; the name is also linked to the 84,000 teachings (beopmun) the blocks are said to contain.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. Every cited URL for all 6 episodes (52 facts) was re-opened (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies when the live site resets connections) and quotes/locators were compared; the one exception is unesco.org/en/prizes/literacy (unreachable from here; its claim is now also backed by a Korean MCST press release). Eight minimal corrections were made: (1) Hangeul Day f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' (no cited source says the October 9 conversion was Gregorian; encykorea separates Julian/Gregorian only for 1932-45) and dates the October 29/28 observances; (2) f10 gains a third source (SBS 2018 with 국립한글박물관 curator); (3) Shapes scene 8, learning goal and f7 now say 'South Korea's spelling rules' count 24 (North Korea counts 40, 국립한글박물관 webzine 59); (4) Sejong scene 4/f4: 백성 is 'an old-fashioned word' with 표준국어대사전 added; (5) Jikji f8 quote no longer repeats a prize amount that differs between UNESCO page versions; (6) Tripitaka f6 wood and corner plates now have two further sources (정책브리핑; 박상진 wood-identification study); (8) Hangeul Day f9 gains a second source (문화체육관광부 press release); (7) Panjeon scene 8/f9: 'visitors cannot walk inside' replaced by 'visitor entry is restricted' because Haeinsa has run pre-booked tours inside Beopbojeon since June 2021. See hangul-printing.signoff.md.

authorNotes: The carving period follows 국가유산포털, 한국민족문화대백과사전 and UNESCO WHC (1237–1248). Some accounts count the whole project, preparation included, as about 16 years ending in 1251, so the narration gives only 1237–1248. The count of 81,258 comes from a survey made under Japanese rule and includes some blocks re-carved in Joseon (국가유산포털), so the narration says 'more than 80,000'. Where the carving took place (Ganghwa versus Namhae) is treated differently across sources and is left out. The 1398 move to Haeinsa appears only on 국가유산포털 pages, so it is left out too. The earlier set of blocks lost to fire in 1232 is left out to keep the war content mild. UNESCO's Memory of the World page places Haeinsa in the 'southwest' of the peninsula, but Haeinsa is in South Gyeongsang Province in the southeast, so that phrase was not used. 'Almost 800 years later' is worked out from 1248. The official heritage name is 합천 해인사 대장경판 (Hapcheon Haeinsa Daejanggyeongpan). REVISED: scene 1 no longer puts Hoya 'inside' the hall (visitor entry is restricted, see story-janggyeong-panjeon). f5 attributes the exact figure 81,258 to UNESCO (verified on the Memory of the World page) and records the Korea Heritage Service caveat; other published counts (about 81,350; 81,352) were reported by one fact-checker but not verified here, so no exact number appears in the narration.
